facts.statement: He was born at Market Rasen, Lincolnshire, on 27 May 1794.
At eighteen he became an ensign in the Cambridgeshire militia; after his marriage to Elizabeth, daughter of Sir John Collins, he lived for about a year in France near Tours and returned home in 1817.
He graduated M.D. at Edinburgh in 1821 with an inaugural thesis on the state of the mind in insanity and melancholia.
After short periods of practice at Lewes and Chichester he settled for about five years at Stratford-upon-Avon, where he was alderman and twice mayor and inspecting physician to the county asylums.
He moved to London in 1827 and in 1828 became professor of the practice of medicine at the new University College.
An Inquiry Concerning the Indications of Insanity appeared in 1830, written while he held the chair.
In 1830 he left London for Warwick, where he again served as inspecting physician to the county asylums, and in 1838 he moved to Birmingham.
He took charge of the Middlesex County Asylum at Hanwell on 1 June 1839; from 21 September 1839 every form of mechanical restraint was discontinued there.
He gave up residence at the asylum in 1844 or 1845 and kept medical control as visiting physician until 1852.
He was elected a Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in 1844 and gave the Croonian Lectures on mania at the College in 1848–49.

With Charles Hastings and John Forbes he took part in founding the Provincial Medical and Surgical Association, later the British Medical Association; the University of Oxford conferred on him the honorary degree of D.C.L. when the Association met there.
His books include On the Construction and Government of Lunatic Asylums (1847), The Treatment of the Insane without Mechanical Restraints (1856) and A Study of Hamlet (1863).
The Treatment of the Insane without Mechanical Restraints was published by Smith, Elder & Co. in London in 1856, dedicated to Sir James Clark and dated from The Lawn House, Hanwell, 26 July 1856.
On his retirement as visiting physician he was presented with a piece of plate and a portrait of himself by Sir John Watson Gordon.
He died in his house at Hanwell on 5 March 1866.

uncertainties.decision: The Dictionary of National Biography gives 1844, Munk's Roll 1845. The page says 1844 or 1845.

Both sources record the honorary D.C.L.; neither gives the year. A date of 21 July 1852, during the Association's meeting at Oxford, appears in secondary accounts but no contemporary record has been seen. The page gives no year.

uncertainties.claim: Years at Lewes, Chichester and Stratford-upon-Avon; years of the two mayoralties
uncertainties.decision: The sources give durations, not dates. The page names the towns and offices without years.

uncertainties.claim: Resignation of the University College chair
uncertainties.decision: No date is given; both sources place his departure from London in 1830. The page does not date the resignation.

Both sources say he owned or managed a private asylum in the village of Hanwell. The 1856 dedication is dated from The Lawn House, Hanwell; that the house was the private asylum is not stated in the sources read, and the page does not say so.
Neither source names it. A gravestone in the Kensington Cemetery at Hanwell is reported in secondary sources and photographs, not in a documentary record seen; the page does not name a burial place.
The Wellcome catalogue gives none. Maull & Polyblank worked as a partnership in London in the 1850s and 1860s; the page does not date the likeness.

uncertainties.claim: Death year in the Wikisource heading
uncertainties.decision: The heading of the Wikisource transcription reads 1794–1860; the article text and Munk's Roll give 5 March 1866, which the page follows.

interpretation.note: Non-restraint is presented as a system Conolly carried through at Hanwell on a large public scale, prepared by the York Retreat and by Gardiner Hill and Charlesworth at Lincoln, not as his sole invention; the book is read as his own account and justification.

appraisal.note: Prose follows the JC_005 publisher's paratext V2 (About the Author) in substance, corrected against the two biographical sources. AETERNUS editorial judgement; no invented quotation.

en.tagline: The physician who took the straps and strait-waistcoats out of Hanwell, and wrote down how it was done.
en.intro: John Conolly, M.D., took charge of the Middlesex County Asylum at Hanwell, an asylum of some eight hundred patients, on 1 June 1839. From 21 September of that year no patient there was put under mechanical restraint. In 1856 he set down the history and the method of that change in The Treatment of the Insane without Mechanical Restraints.
en.orientation: Conolly did not invent non-restraint. The York Retreat and the Lincoln asylum had prepared the ground. What he showed was that a public asylum of several hundred patients could be governed without chains, belts and strait-waistcoats, if attendants, wards, occupation and supervision were organised to replace them. His book treats non-restraint as a discipline for the staff as much as a mercy to the patients.
overview: Before Hanwell his career was uncertain: militia officer, provincial physician and mayor, a London professor who left his chair after two years. His interest in insanity reached back to his Edinburgh thesis of 1821 and to his posts as inspecting physician to the Warwickshire asylums.
After Hanwell he was consulted as an authority on the care of the insane, and he wrote on how asylums should be built and governed.

origin: John Conolly was born at Market Rasen in Lincolnshire on 27 May 1794. At eighteen he became an ensign in the Cambridgeshire militia. After his marriage to Elizabeth, daughter of Sir John Collins, he spent about a year in France, near Tours, and returned home in 1817 to study medicine at Edinburgh.
He graduated M.D. in 1821. His inaugural thesis dealt with the state of the mind in insanity and melancholia, the subject that would decide his later career.
career: After short periods of practice at Lewes and Chichester he settled at Stratford-upon-Avon for about five years. He was alderman and twice mayor of the borough and inspecting physician to the county asylums. In 1827 he moved to London, and in 1828 he became professor of the practice of medicine at the newly founded University College. An Inquiry Concerning the Indications of Insanity appeared in 1830. In the same year he left London for Warwick, where he again inspected the county asylums. In 1838 he moved to Birmingham. With Charles Hastings and John Forbes he helped to found the Provincial Medical and Surgical Association, later the British Medical Association.

On 1 June 1839 he took charge of the Middlesex County Asylum at Hanwell, and from 21 September every form of mechanical restraint was discontinued there. He gave up residence in 1844 or 1845 and remained visiting physician until 1852. On his retirement he was presented with a piece of plate and a portrait of himself by Sir John Watson Gordon. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in 1844, gave the Croonian Lectures on mania in 1848–49, and received an honorary D.C.L. from the University of Oxford. In his later years he had a large consulting practice in mental disease and a private asylum in the village of Hanwell. He died in his house at Hanwell on 5 March 1866.
literature: On the Construction and Government of Lunatic Asylums (1847) set out how an asylum should be built and run. The Treatment of the Insane without Mechanical Restraints (1856) is his account of the change itself: the last days of the old methods, the first experiments at Lincoln, the abolition of restraint at Hanwell in 1839, its adoption in the large English asylums and its reception on the Continent. He dedicated it to Sir James Clark and dated it from The Lawn House, Hanwell, 26 July 1856.

The book is the testimony and the defence of the man who carried the system through. It describes the old instruments of restraint precisely, and it is just as exact about what was put in their place: watchful attendants, seclusion used with care, occupation, regular meals and the daily visits of the physician on the wards. In A Study of Hamlet (1863) he turned the same experience to Shakespeare's play.
en.legacy: Conolly's distinction lies in showing, on a large public scale and in print, that mechanical coercion was not necessary to the government of an asylum. His own system kept considerable powers of control, and the book should be read with that in mind. The standard it set for English asylums nevertheless held.
en.bridge: The Treatment of the Insane without Mechanical Restraints (1856). An English AETERNUS edition following the London text of 1856, with a new medical and historical apparatus, is in preparation in the Anthracite Series.
en.description: John Conolly, M.D. (1794–1866), resident physician at the Middlesex County Asylum at Hanwell, who abolished mechanical restraint there in 1839, and author of The Treatment of the Insane without Mechanical Restraints (1856). An English AETERNUS edition is in preparation.
